title: Shared jeeps from NJP and around the Darjeeling hills
meta_description: How shared jeeps work from NJP and Siliguri to Darjeeling, Kurseong and Mirik, and onward to Kalimpong, Gangtok and Manebhanjan: stands, fares, timings.
summary: Shared jeeps are how the Darjeeling hills move. Ten seats, a fixed fare per seat and a departure when full: ₹250–400 from NJP to Darjeeling against ₹3,500–4,500 for a reserved car, indicative 2026. Go in the morning, buy your seat at the counter, sit in the middle row and keep a spare hour on the return.

sections.heading: How a shared jeep works
paras: The hill jeep is a Tata Sumo, Mahindra Bolero or similar, licensed to carry about ten passengers: two beside the driver, four in the middle row and four on the side benches or bench at the back. Each route has a stand and a drivers' syndicate that fixes the fare, keeps a queue of vehicles and sells tickets at a counter or from a man with a notebook. You buy a seat, your bag goes on the roof under a tarpaulin, and the jeep leaves when all seats are sold.

That last point matters. A jeep does not run to a timetable. In the morning on busy routes, it may fill in five minutes. In the afternoon, on quiet routes, you may wait an hour, or be asked to pay for empty seats to leave now. Buying all ten seats is called reserving the jeep, and it is how many families travel: the price is roughly ten times the seat fare, usually a little less than a private taxi.

Shared jeeps carry everyone: schoolteachers, monks, tea-garden managers, families with sacks of rice and travellers like you. It is safe, ordinary transport, and the drivers know these roads better than anyone.

sections.heading: Routes and fares at a glance
paras: These are the main routes travellers use, with indicative 2026 seat fares and times. Fares follow fuel prices and are revised from time to time, and syndicates sometimes add a little in peak weeks. Treat them as a guide and check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: From NJP and Siliguri: where to find them
paras: At New Jalpaiguri station, walk out of the main exit to the forecourt. Drivers and touts call out Darjeeling, Gangtok and Kalimpong; the syndicate counters and parked jeeps are just beyond. Morning trains from Kolkata arrive between about 6 and 9 am, and that is when jeeps fill fastest. Ask the price at the counter, not from a tout, and pay only there.

In Siliguri town, jeeps for Darjeeling, Kurseong and Mirik leave from the stands along Hill Cart Road, around the Tenzing Norgay Central Bus Terminus. Jeeps and buses for Gangtok leave from the Sikkim Nationalised Transport terminus on the same road. If you land at Bagdogra, take a prepaid or app cab, ₹300–600, to the Hill Cart Road stands or NJP and start from there.

The ride up to Darjeeling goes either by the Rohini road, faster and full of bends, or by Hill Cart Road through Kurseong, slower and with views of the toy-train track. The driver decides. The jeep stops once, usually at Kurseong or near Rohini, for tea and toilets.

sections.heading: In Darjeeling: the motor stands
paras: Darjeeling's shared jeeps leave from the motor stands in and around Chowk Bazaar, below Laden La Road and the Old Super Market complex. Each destination has its own syndicate counter: Siliguri and NJP, Kurseong, Mirik, Kalimpong, Gangtok, Manebhanjan, Sukhiapokhri and others. Ask anyone for the counter you need; it can be confusing the first time, because the stand is crowded and steep.

Buy your seat a day ahead in season, especially for Gangtok and Siliguri on Sundays and at the end of holidays. Counters open early, around 6 am, and most long-distance jeeps run between 6.30 am and 2 pm. Short local routes, such as Ghum or Jorebunglow, run all day from the stands and from the roadside on Hill Cart Road.

Note the difference between shared jeeps and the local taxis at the Club Side stand on Gandhi Road and around Chowrasta. Local taxis do sightseeing tours and short hops at fixed rates per car. They are not shared, though your hotel can sometimes put you with another group for Tiger Hill.

sections.heading: Tips for a better ride
paras: A few habits make shared jeeps much more comfortable, and they cost nothing.
list: Ask for a middle-row seat. The front two seats are the most comfortable and sometimes cost a little more; the back benches are cramped and bounce on bends.
If you get car sick, sit in front or by a middle window, eat lightly and take a tablet 30 minutes before.
Buy two seats for one person if you want space or have a big bag; drivers are happy to sell them.
Keep valuables, water and a jacket on your lap. Bags on the roof are tied down and covered, but they can get dusty or wet.
Carry small notes and UPI on your phone; counters prefer exact change.
Leave Darjeeling by 11 am for an evening train or flight. Traffic builds through Kurseong and Rohini in the afternoon and jams at Siliguri.
On strike or bandh days, jeeps do not run. Ask your hotel the evening before.

sections.heading: When a reserved car makes more sense
paras: Shared jeeps are not always the cheapest choice per head. A family of four or five with luggage pays ₹1,250–2,000 in seats from NJP to Darjeeling, against ₹3,500–4,500 for a reserved small car or Bolero, indicative 2026. For a small extra cost you leave when you want, stop where you like and do not wait for the jeep to fill.

A reserved car also makes sense for early mornings, such as Tiger Hill at 4 am, for late arrivals when shared jeeps have stopped, for elderly travellers who find climbing into the back row hard, and for routes with few shared departures, such as the villages of Sittong, Chatakpur and Lepchajagat. Even then, mix: go up by shared jeep, hire a car only for the sightseeing day, and come down by jeep again.

Whatever you choose, agree the price before you get in, ask whether parking and tolls are included, and confirm the drop point. Many drivers in Darjeeling stop at the motor stand below town, not at hotel doors above Chowrasta, because cars cannot enter the upper Mall.

sections.heading: Going further: Kalimpong, Gangtok and the trails
paras: From Darjeeling, morning jeeps run to Kalimpong by the Peshok road through Lopchu and Teesta Bazaar, and to Gangtok via Teesta Bazaar and Melli, joining NH10 into Sikkim at Rangpo. Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit for Gangtok and should tell the driver, who will stop at the Rangpo checkpost; Indians need only photo ID. Check current status before you travel.

For the Sandakphu trek, jeeps run from Darjeeling to Manebhanjan, the trailhead, from early morning. For the return, jeeps leave Rimbik and Srikhola for Darjeeling in the morning and early afternoon; seats are limited, so ask your guide to book one. For Mirik, jeeps from Darjeeling go via Ghum, Lepchajagat and Sukhiapokhri; they will drop you at Lepchajagat on the way for a small fare.

One more option is the bus. North Bengal State Transport Corporation buses run between Siliguri, Darjeeling, Kurseong and Mirik at lower fares than jeeps, but they are slower and fewer. They suit travellers with time and a sense of adventure.

faqs.q: How much is a shared jeep from NJP to Darjeeling
faqs.a: A seat costs about ₹250–400, indicative 2026, depending on season and seat. The front seats sometimes cost more. Jeeps leave from outside NJP station and from the Hill Cart Road stands in Siliguri, and take 3–3.5 hours. Fares follow fuel prices and syndicate revisions, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What time do shared jeeps leave NJP for Darjeeling
faqs.a: There is no fixed timetable; jeeps leave when full. They run most often from about 6 am to 2 pm, especially after morning trains from Kolkata arrive. After mid-afternoon departures thin out and you may need to pay for empty seats or hire a car. Try to reach NJP before 1 pm.

faqs.q: Where is the shared jeep stand in Darjeeling
faqs.a: Shared jeeps leave from the motor stands in and around Chowk Bazaar, below Laden La Road and near the Old Super Market complex. Each destination has its own counter. From Chowrasta it is a 10–15 minute walk downhill. Buy tickets a day ahead in season for Siliguri, Gangtok and Kalimpong.

faqs.q: Is a shared jeep safe for women travelling alone
faqs.a: Yes. Local women use shared jeeps every day, and they are ordinary public transport in the hills. Sit in the front or middle row, keep your bag on your lap and travel in daylight. Buy from the official counter. If anything makes you uncomfortable, tell the counter staff, who know the drivers.

faqs.q: Can I book a shared jeep online
faqs.a: Generally no. Seats are sold at the stand counters on the day or a day ahead. Some hotels and travel desks will buy a seat for you for a small fee. Some app-based and private shared-cab services run between Siliguri and Darjeeling, but rules and availability change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much is a reserved car from NJP to Darjeeling
faqs.a: About ₹3,500–4,500 for a small car or Bolero, indicative 2026, and more for an Innova. It takes about 3 hours. For a family of four or five with luggage, a reserved car costs only a little more than buying all the seats in a shared jeep, and you can leave when you want.

faqs.q: Is there a shared jeep from Darjeeling to Gangtok
faqs.a: Yes. Morning jeeps run from the Darjeeling motor stand to Gangtok for about ₹400–550 a seat, indicative 2026, taking 4.5–5 hours via Teesta Bazaar, Melli and Rangpo. Buy a day ahead. Foreign nationals must carry their Sikkim permit or obtain it at Rangpo. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I carry big luggage in a shared jeep
faqs.a: Yes. Bags go on the roof, tied and covered with a tarpaulin. Very large suitcases may cost an extra seat or a small fee. Keep valuables, medicines and a jacket with you inside. In the monsoon, wrap bags in plastic, as roof covers do not always keep out heavy rain.

faqs.q: Do shared jeeps run during a bandh in Darjeeling
faqs.a: No. During a bandh or general strike, shared jeeps, taxis and most shops stop. Bandhs are less common than in the past but still happen. Hotels and local news give notice a day or two ahead. Keep a spare day before an important train or flight and check current status before you travel.
